title: 🪙 Economy, Trade & Material Life
rawNotionMarkup: Eryndor's economy is a living system. Prices respond to local supply and demand, season, harvests, weather, war, transport routes, tolls, taxes, shortages, quality, reputation and the wealth of the buyer or establishment. Prices below are grounded starting points where recorded, not permanent universal tariffs. ## Currency and accounting The standard Eryndoran currency system is now established as a four-denomination system: | Coin | Conversion to lower denomination | | --- | --- | | 1 Copper piece | Base unit | | 1 Silver crown | 100 copper | | 1 Gold crown | 100 silver = 10,000 copper | | 1 Platinum crown | 100 gold = 10,000 silver = 1,000,000 copper | The standard exchange is therefore 100 copper = 1 silver, 100 silver = 1 gold, and 100 gold = 1 platinum. This is the default conversion across Eryndor. ### Typical use - Copper: Everyday purchases, small meals, drinks, minor services and market goods. - Silver: Ordinary wages, lodging, routine equipment and larger everyday transactions. - Gold: Expensive goods, fine equipment, property-related payments, substantial contracts and major commercial transactions. - Platinum: Exceptionally large transfers, royal treasuries, major institutional payments and transactions involving immense wealth. Platinum coinage is rare in ordinary circulation. These are usage tendencies, not legal restrictions. A wealthy merchant may pay in silver, and a small shop may refuse or be unable to make change for a gold or platinum coin. ### Regional variation The conversion above is the standard accounting value across Eryndor. Different kingdoms, thrones and republics may use different coin names, designs, weights, mint marks and local customs. Regional exchange rates, debasement, clipping, counterfeit risk and the practical value of foreign coin may vary and should be established when relevant. Do not assume every settlement accepts every denomination at face value. Gloin's existing ledger remains denominated in silver crowns and copper pieces. Convert to gold or platinum only when an actual transaction makes it useful; do not retroactively alter his recorded wealth. ### Change record This four-denomination system was explicitly approved during the Compendium reconstruction. It expands the earlier reference, which had only formally recorded copper and silver. When tracking money: - Record starting funds, income, purchases, wages, rents, deposits, debts, taxes and sale proceeds. - Never silently deduct money. - State meaningful prices before or when the player commits to a purchase, rental or contract. - Record recurring costs only when the character actually takes them on. - Buying and selling are not automatically at the same price. Merchants need a margin, and condition, demand, reputation and bargaining matter. - Preserve exact balances and use arithmetic carefully. ## Karak-Varn baseline prices The following are agreed starting prices for ordinary goods and services in Karak-Varn. They are not universal across Eryndor. | Good or service | Typical price | | --- | --- | | Shared common-room bed | 2 copper per night | | Basic private room | 5 copper per night | | Comfortable private room | 8 copper per night | | Quality inn room | 1 silver per night | | Bath and hot water | 2 copper | | Simple breakfast | 2–3 copper | | Hearty breakfast | 5 copper | | Hearty meal | 4–6 copper | | Small ale | 2 copper | | Autumn honey brew | 3 copper | Better inns, festivals, busy market days, shortages or unusual services can raise prices. Quiet periods, competition, poor conditions or negotiated arrangements may lower them. ## Trade goods and materials Track prices when goods become relevant to play. Categories include: - Food and agriculture: grain, flour, bread, meat, fish, vegetables, fruit, dairy, preserved foods, livestock and animal feed. - Drink: ale, beer, mead, honey brews, wine, spirits, tea and local beverages. - Raw materials: iron, copper, tin, silver, gold, coal, timber, stone, leather, wool, salt, clay, glass sand and other useful materials. - Craft goods: tools, weapons, armour, clothing, boots, pottery, furniture, household wares, machinery, runic components and finished craftwork. - Transport and services: pack animals, carts, freight, ferries, stabling, repairs, skilled labour, healing, training, storage, guides and lodging. - Property and rents: rooms, workshops, stalls, storage space, homes, farmland, leases, deposits, upkeep and local fees or taxes. Do not invent a complete price catalogue before goods matter. Establish a sensible local baseline when a character encounters or needs an item, record it and use it consistently until circumstances change. ## Major trade patterns These are established broad trade tendencies, not exclusive monopolies or claims that every region exports only these goods. - Khazari: Iron, steel, machinery, weapons, stonework, mining equipment and engineered craft. - Eldar: Fine textiles, enchanted materials, medicines and specialist craft. - Urakai: Livestock, metals, equipment and agricultural goods. - Merchant Republics: Ships, luxury goods, finance and trade services. - Southern Sultanates: Spices, dyes, precious materials and textiles. Trade flows in both directions. Imports, local production, competing suppliers, tariffs, credit, transport costs and diplomatic conditions shape actual markets. ## How prices fluctuate ### Supply and demand Shortages tend to raise prices; surplus and competition tend to lower them. A shortage should have a cause—harvest failure, disrupted transport, exhausted mines, hoarding, war demand, disease or another grounded event. ### Season and harvest Food, fuel, animal feed and some raw materials vary with season and harvest quality. Weather can damage crops, delay shipments or close routes. ### War and politics Mobilisation can increase demand for metal, weapons, armour, horses, food, transport, fortifications and skilled labour. Blockades, tariffs, border tension or occupation can disrupt supply and raise delivered prices. ### Transport and geography Distance, dangerous roads, mountain passes, weather, tolls, security escorts and transfer points affect price. A good available locally may cost substantially more when imported. ### Quality and scarcity Common, serviceable, fine, masterwork, rare and enchanted goods should not share one price. Material quality, craftsmanship, condition, provenance and reputation all matter. ### Local conditions and time District, town size, wealth, taxes, guild rules, establishment quality and bargaining affect the final price. Prices may change between visits, but changes should have a cause in the world rather than fluctuating randomly to punish or reward the player. ## Wages, contracts and livelihoods Eryndor's economy includes farmers, labourers, miners, smiths, artisans, merchants, sailors, clerks, healers, teachers, guards, soldiers, couriers, guides and specialist practitioners. Their earnings depend on region, experience, status, risk, demand, season and bargaining. Potential ways a character may earn income include smithing, mine or engineering work, guard and mercenary contracts, repairs, gathering, hauling, guiding and specialist work as skills improve. Work is not guaranteed to be available, and a job's pay, danger, time, tools and obligations should be established before acceptance. A wage should reflect: - Skill, experience and quality of work. - Time and effort required. - Materials, tools and equipment supplied by each party. - Risk, urgency, travel and working conditions. - Local demand, employer resources and bargaining. - Whether the job is casual labour, apprenticeship, contract work or specialist service. ## Economic consequences in the living world Economic developments can affect ordinary lives and political choices. A rise in iron prices may help some mines and smiths while increasing costs for farmers, builders, guards and armies. A blocked Deepway route may delay ore and grain, reduce guild income and increase prices in distant markets. A good harvest may lower food prices but reduce the earnings of some producers. Economic change should have winners, losers, adaptation and knock-on effects. Do not treat markets as a background number divorced from people's lives. ## Accounting and play rules - Track the player's money and possessions precisely. - State prices clearly and allow the player to choose whether to pay, negotiate or walk away. - Do not infer a purchase from interest, asking a price or inspecting an item. - Do not invent wages, tips, refunds or sale proceeds. - Keep rumours about shortages distinct from confirmed market conditions. - Consider recurring rent, food, stable fees, storage, maintenance and taxes only when they are actually incurred. - Preserve the difference between a price quote, a negotiated agreement and a completed transaction. The Karak-Varn list is a working baseline. Other cities, ports, villages, military camps and remote communities need their own local conditions.
